definition: Cybercheck is a generative AI tool that purports to identify the perpetrators of crime through geolocation with "90% accuracy." It has been used in thousands of criminal cases across the United States, including death penalty cases, but serious doubts have been raised about its accuracy and reliability.
details: Its creator, Adam Mosher, has repeatedly declined to explain how the technology works, claiming that it is proprietary software. Mosher has said under oath that Cybercheck does not retain records of where it obtains its data, how it makes connections between data points or how it calculates its accuracy ratings. In some jurisdictions, including a case in Colorado, judges ruled evidence produced by Cybercheck inadmissible, and charges were dropped as a result. In April of 2024, lawyers in Akron, Ohio accused Mosher of lying under oath. The most well covered case employing Cybercheck is that of the 2022 conviction of Adarus Black, who was given a life sentence after being accused of a drive-by shooting, despite a lack of direct evidence. Jurors said their decision was based entirely on Mosher's testimony. It is currently the subject of a CBC Uncover investigation.

explainer.lead: Cybercheck claims to use geolocation to identify crime suspects, and its results have been used in thousands of US criminal cases, including death penalty cases. Its asserted 90% accuracy, undisclosed methods, and missing records make its outputs difficult to examine, with serious consequences for defendants and courts.

tiers.eli5: Imagine someone says they can solve a mystery using a map, but will not show where their clues came from or how they checked the answer. Cybercheck says it can find crime suspects this way and claims to be right 90% of the time. Courts have sometimes rejected its evidence because its work cannot be properly explained or checked.
tiers.practitioner: Cybercheck is applied as a forensic investigative tool, with geolocation-based findings and Adam Mosher's testimony used in criminal proceedings. Its central pitfalls are absent data-lineage records, undisclosed linkage methods, and an undocumented accuracy calculation, which prevent reconstruction of an output. Evidence has been ruled inadmissible in some jurisdictions, including a Colorado case where charges were subsequently dropped.
tiers.paperLevel: Cybercheck can be represented as a claimed inference function f(data) -> suspected perpetrator using geolocation, with an asserted accuracy of 90%; Mosher has said under oath that it does not retain records of its data origins, connections between data points, or accuracy calculations. Its operating method remains undisclosed, and its reliability has been challenged in court, including an April 2024 accusation by Akron, Ohio lawyers that Mosher lied under oath.

explainer.example: In 2022, Adarus Black was convicted of a drive-by shooting and sentenced to life despite a lack of direct evidence. Jurors said their decision was based entirely on Adam Mosher's testimony about Cybercheck.

explainer.intuition: The idea is to turn geolocation information into an identification of whoever committed a crime. The difficulty is that the claimed answer cannot be readily audited when the data origins, reasoning process, and accuracy calculation are unavailable.
howItWorks: Cybercheck uses data whose origins it does not record.
It applies geolocation to investigate a crime and identify a perpetrator.
It makes connections between data points through an undisclosed process.
Its output is presented with a claimed accuracy of 90%, calculated by an undocumented method.
Its findings can enter court through evidence and Mosher's testimony.
explainer.whyItMatters: An opaque identification can affect liberty or even life when used in criminal and death penalty cases. Judicial rejections of Cybercheck evidence, including a Colorado ruling followed by dropped charges, show how reliability and explainability can determine whether a case proceeds.
misconceptions: The 90% figure is a demonstrated accuracy measurement rather than a claim whose calculation is undocumented.
A Cybercheck identification counts as direct evidence of a crime.
Its findings can be reconstructed from retained records of its data and reasoning.
